items.title: Immediate decompression of tension pneumothorax
items.contentHtml:
Tension pneumothorax

  • Clinical diagnosis: unilateral absence of breath sounds, tympanism, contralateral tracheal deviation, hypotension, jugular distension; do not wait for radiography if there is instability.
  • Immediate decompression: thick needle (14-16 G) in second intercostal space midclavicular line or fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line; If there is no improvement, consider immediate thoracostomy.
  • Pathophysiology: valvular mechanism that traps air, increases intrapleural pressure, collapses the lung and displaces the mediastinum; compromised venous return and cardiac output.
  • After needle: always place a chest tube; the needle is a temporary bridge.
  • Examination trap: needle decompression in the 2nd space fails in up to 30-50% due to wall thickness in obese patients; use 5th space as an alternative.

items.title: Massive hemothorax: chest tube
items.contentHtml:
Massive hemothorax

  • Definition: rapid accumulation of >1500 mL of blood in the pleural cavity or active bleeding (200 mL/h for 2-4 h).
  • First line: drainage with chest tube (caliber 36-40 Fr) in fifth intercostal space medial axillary; monitor initial and hourly output.
  • Indication for thoracotomy: initial drainage >1500 mL or >200 mL/h for 2-4 hours; sudden release of blood with instability.
  • Autotransfusion: consider sterile blood without abdominal contamination.
  • Trap: massive hemothorax can present with hypotension without tracheal deviation; the x-ray may show complete opacity, but the diagnosis is clinical-ultrasound (FAST).

items.foco: Unstable chest management with mechanical ventilation
items.title: Flail chest: mechanical ventilation
items.contentHtml:
Flatable chest

  • Definition: fracture of ≥2 ribs in ≥2 sites that produces paradoxical movement of the chest wall; the underlying injury is pulmonary contusion.
  • Initial management: oxygen, analgesia, respiratory physiotherapy; mechanical ventilation is reserved for persistent hypoxemia or hypercapnia despite optimal analgesia.
  • Intubation criteria: PaO2 <60 mmHg, PaCO2 >50 mmHg, respiratory rate >35/min, neurological deterioration, shock.
  • Ventilatory mode: prefer ventilation with pressure support or volume controlled with PEEP to recruit alveoli; avoid barotrauma.
  • Trap: surgical fixation of ribs is indicated in weaning failure or severe, non-routine deformity.

items.foco: Lung contusion hypoxemia does not respond to oxygen
items.title: Lung contusion: refractory hypoxemia
items.contentHtml:
Pulmonary contusion

  • Pathophysiology: alveolar damage due to shock wave, edema and hemorrhage; hypoxemia worsens in 24-48 hours.
  • Diagnosis: chest x-ray shows patchy non-segmental infiltrates; CT scan is more sensitive.
  • Management: supplemental oxygen, analgesia, physical therapy; if hypoxemia does not respond to oxygen, use non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation with PEEP.
  • Fluids: fluid restriction to avoid overload; use diuretics if there is edema without hypovolemia.
  • Trap: pulmonary contusion may progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome; Do not confuse with pneumothorax.

items.foco: Rib fractures analgesia and respiratory physiotherapy
items.title: Rib fractures: analgesia and physiotherapy
items.contentHtml:
Rib fractures

  • Objective: prevent atelectasis and pneumonia through analgesia and respiratory physiotherapy.
  • Stepped analgesia: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400-800 mg every 8 h), paracetamol 1 g every 6-8 h; opioids if severe pain.
  • Blocks: paravertebral block or thoracic epidural block are the choice in multiple fractures or unstable chest.
  • Physiotherapy: incentive spirometer, directed cough, early ambulation.
  • Trap: morphine can depress breathing; prefer regional blocks to avoid hypoventilation.

items.title: Traumatic aortic injury: mediastinal widening
items.contentHtml:
Thoracic aorta injury

  • Mechanism: sudden deceleration, typical in high-speed accidents; the most common site is the aortic isthmus (distal to the left subclavian). chest with contrast; transesophageal echocardiography if unstable.
  • Initial management: blood pressure control with beta blocker (esmolol) and vasodilator (nitroprusside) if hypertension, then endovascular or surgical repair.
  • Trap: the absence of mediastinal widening does not exclude minor aortic injury.

items.title: Tracheobronchial rupture: persistent air leak
items.contentHtml:
Tracheobronchial rupture

  • Presentation: subcutaneous emphysema, tension pneumothorax, hemoptysis, persistent air leak after chest tube (continuous bubbling during aspiration).
  • Diagnosis: flexible bronchoscopy is the gold standard; X-ray may show pulmonary collapse with signs of lung collapse.
  • Management: selective intubation to the healthy bronchus if possible; early surgical repair (primary suture or resection).
  • Trap: air leak that does not subside with correct aspiration and patent tube suggests proximal injury; do not remove the tube without bronchoscopy.

items.foco: Cardiac tamponade pericardial window or thoracotomy
items.title: Cardiac tamponade: drainage or thoracotomy
items.contentHtml:
Cardiac tamponade

  • Beck's triad: hypotension, jugular distension, muffled heart sounds; also paradoxical pulse.
  • Diagnosis: echocardiography or FAST (pericardial effusion, diastolic collapse of the right atrium).
  • Initial management: ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis as a bridge; if instability persists, subxiphoid pericardial window or emergency thoracotomy. Indication for thoracotomy: tamponade due to penetrating wound with arrest or severe instability; requires surgeon.
  • Trap: pericardiocentesis can fail due to clots; the pericardial window is more effective.

items.foco: Indication for emergency thoracotomy in trauma
items.title: Emergency thoracotomy: indications
items.contentHtml:
Emergency thoracotomy

  • Indications: cardiac arrest witnessed in penetrating trauma with previous vital signs; refractory hypotension after drainage of massive hemothorax; acute cardiac tamponade.
  • Contraindications: blunt trauma with arrest without vital signs; absence of pulseless electrical activity for >10 minutes; penetrating trauma with arrest without vital signs in the field.
  • Maneuvers: left anterolateral thoracotomy, opening of the pericardium, hemorrhage control, direct cardiac massage, descending aorta clamping.
  • Survival: greater in penetrating cardiac injuries; minor in blunt trauma.
  • Trap: do not perform if there is no trained surgeon or resources to continue.

items.foco: Broken scapula sign in penetrating trauma
items.title: Broken scapula: penetrating trauma
items.contentHtml:
Broken scapula sign

  • Definition: fracture of the scapula in a penetrating wound indicates that the object passed through the thorax; high probability of vascular or visceral injuries.
  • Interpretation: the scapula protects the posterior wall; His fracture suggests a transfixing path with lung, mediastinal or great vessel damage.
  • Management: chest angiotomography to rule out vascular injury; surgical exploration if there is instability or bleeding.
  • Trap: do not underestimate isolated scapular fracture in penetrating trauma; look for associated injury.

items.title: Open pneumothorax: three-point dressing
items.contentHtml:
Open pneumothorax

  • Definition: wound in the chest wall that connects the pleural cavity with the outside, with a diameter >2/3 of the tracheal diameter; produces air entry through the wound.
  • Initial management: place three-point dressing (occlusive fixed on three sides) to allow air to escape and avoid tension pneumothorax.
  • Afterwards: chest tube at a distance from the wound, then definitive surgical closure.
  • Trap: do not use complete occlusive dressing (four points) because it becomes tension pneumothorax.

items.foco: Bronchopleural fistula secondary to penetrating trauma
items.title: Traumatic bronchopleural fistula
items.contentHtml:
Bronchopleural fistula

  • Definition: anomalous communication between the bronchial tree and the pleural space, secondary to penetrating injury or tracheobronchial rupture.
  • Manifestation: persistent air leak through the chest tube, subcutaneous emphysema, recurrent pneumothorax after removal of tube.
  • Diagnosis: bronchoscopy to locate the leak; x-ray with suction tube shows continuous bubbling.
  • Management: chest tube with suction, surgical repair (suture or resection) if it does not close; consider bronchial stent in selected cases.
  • Trap: persistent leak >48-72 hours after adequate drainage suggests fistula; Do not remove tube without resolution.
